subject: Business Models
title: WeWork: Growth at Any Cost
description: Learn WeWork: Growth at Any Cost in one minute.

hook.text: WeWork was valued at $47 billion in 2019. After its failed IPO, it was worth $8 billion. A 83% collapse.

buildup.text: WeWork signed long-term building leases and subleased desks on short-term contracts. It called this 'community.'

discovery.text: WeWork's model is simple: arbitrage between long and short lease terms. It's a real estate company, not a tech unicorn.

twist.text: CEO Adam Neumann cashed out $700 million before the collapse. The founder profited; the company nearly died.

climax.text: WeWork's 2023 bankruptcy proved that calling a real estate business 'tech' doesn't change the underlying economics.

punchline.text: $47B to bankruptcy. WeWork was real estate cosplaying as tech.

quiz.question: What was WeWork's actual business model beneath the 'tech' branding?
options: Lease arbitrage between long and short-term real estate contracts

details.summary: WeWork raised 12 billion dollars to become the most valuable startup in America by rebranding office subleasing as a technology company. When its IPO filing revealed massive losses, irrational spending, and governance failures, the valuation collapsed from 47 billion to under 10 billion.
details.whyItMatters: WeWork exposed how charismatic leadership and tech-company framing inflated a real estate business to absurd valuations..
takeaways: WeWork lost money on every leased space while spending heavily on growth
Positioning as a tech company inflated valuation far beyond real estate norms
IPO filing revelations collapsed the valuation from 47 billion to below 10 billion

faq.question: Why was WeWork valued so highly before its IPO attempt?
faq.answer: SoftBank's Vision Fund led massive funding rounds based on projections of network effects and technology-company growth rates. The narrative positioned WeWork as a platform rather than a landlord, justifying tech-sector valuation multiples on a real estate business.

faq.question: What governance problems did the WeWork IPO filing reveal?
faq.answer: CEO Adam Neumann had trademarked the word We and charged the company 5.9 million for rights to use it, had personal loans from WeWork, controlled super-voting shares, leased his own properties to the company, and had extraordinary power without accountability.
